extracted.intended_audience: students in journalism/media studies (high school or college)
extracted.subtask_description: A classroom activity and checklist for identifying, analyzing, and critiquing Video News Releases (VNRs) distributed by PR firms, with emphasis on ethics and how VNRs are used in broadcast news. Students watch multiple VNRs, answer guided questions, and compare VNR content to local/national news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/Identification of a VNR
rubrics_metrics.description: A Video News Release (VNR) is a ready-made, pre-packaged story—produced in broadcast news style—that is distributed by a PR firm to news stations across the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize VNRs as prepared stories created for clients and produced by PR professionals (often former journalists). Use this definition as the baseline for deciding whether a video is a VNR versus original newsroom reporting. (Text: 'VIDEO NEWS RELEASE ( VNR): A ready-made, pre-packaged story—produced in broadcast news style—that is distributed by a PR firm to news stations across the country.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of PR Newswire / sourcing procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate VNRs by using a national distribution service such as PR Newswire (Multimedia News → Video News) to find recent VNRs and their format icons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the activity: go to www.prnewswire.com, click 'Multimedia News' then 'Video News'. Note the icons indicating formats (audio, video, print) and click the camera icon to view VNRs. (Text: 'PR Newswire is a national news service that distributes multimedia press releases over the Internet.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size / review requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch and review a substantive sample of VNRs to form reliable observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The assignment specifies watching/reviewing 10–20 VNRs to gather evidence and patterns across multiple releases ('Click the camera icon and watch/review 10-20 VNRs').

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational analysis (what stands out)
rubrics_metrics.description: Document immediate observations about each VNR: what you notice and what stands out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-ended descriptive notes: visual style, tone, voiceover, presence/absence of byline or credits, staged interviews, B-roll, statistics, language, and overall production values. Use the prompt: 'What observations can you make about this particular VNR? What do you notice? What stands out to you?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the payer/sponsor and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine who paid for the VNR (company, agency, government) and cite evidence supporting that conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer 'Who is paying for the VNR? (e.g., Six Flags... How do you know?)' — look for explicit credits, corporate logos, branded visuals, spokespersons, language that mirrors client messaging, contact info, or distribution metadata to identify the sponsor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the constructed 'news' event
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what 'news' event has been constructed within the VNR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer 'What ‘news’ event has been constructed in this VNR?' — identify the central narrative or pseudo-event the PR firm frames as news (product launch, study release, community event, safety announcement, etc.). Note how the event is scaffolded to appear timely or urgent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques used to make the event 'newsworthy'
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the specific PR techniques used to make the constructed event seem newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer 'What techniques has the company used in constructing their event to make it ‘newsworthy’?' — catalog tactics such as staged scenes, emotional appeals, expert soundbites, selective statistics, dramatic B-roll, manufactured timeliness, use of former-journalist production style, and authoritative visuals or endorsements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting VNR footage reused in news broadcasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify instances where local or national news uses VNR footage and provide justification for why footage is believed to originate from a VNR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tape news over several days and compare; bring tapes to class and explain why you think footage is from a VNR—look for identical footage, branded shots, matching B-roll, credit lines, identical phrasing or visuals, or absence of newsroom reporter presence. (Text: 'Tape local and national news over the course of several days. Try to identify the use of video news release footage. Bring your tape to class to explain why you think footage is from a VNR.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of labeling/attribution transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether news outlets label VNR content on-air and whether the source/payer is made clear to audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to the normative claim that stations should either avoid using VNRs or, if they use them, label them on-air identifying who provided and paid for them. Use the provided quote and consider ethical standards: 'Not labeling fake news produced by the government or corporations... constitutes news fraud, plagiarism, and violates the most basic ethical standards of journalism.' (John Stauber)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical evaluation — responsibility for disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess which party (the company, the PR firm, or journalists) bears responsibility for informing the public that material is a VNR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss and defend a position in response to 'Who has the greatest responsibility to tell us that VNRs are regularly used – the company (or government), PR firm, or journalists?' Consider journalistic ethics, institutional transparency, and the PR industry's incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of VNRs as a news source
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether a VNR should be considered a valid news source and how it differs from journalist-produced reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the prompt 'Is a VNR a valid news source? What makes a VNR different from a news report done by journalists?' Compare sourcing, independence, editorial control, verification, and attribution practices to assess credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of government-produced VNRs and democratic implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the practice of government agencies distributing VNRs in light of the free press's role as a check on power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to the prompt linking government VNR distribution to the origins and functions of a free press and review the referenced Barstow/Stein NY Times reporting. Consider whether government-produced VNRs undermine or align with democratic accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing the role of public relations in democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect on how public relations activities (including VNRs) influence public opinion, news information, and public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use background statements (e.g., PR industry's mission is to influence public opinion; PR employs many people and handles corporate and government clients) to evaluate positive and negative democratic consequences, such as agenda-setting, information distortion, or public education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of supporting sources and further reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate referenced news articles and analyses to contextualize and support evaluations of VNRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The handout lists related newspaper stories and analyses (e.g., 'The Art of Manufactured News', USA TODAY, NPR, Barstow/Stein NYT). Students should read these to inform ethical and empirical judgments about VNR prevalence and impact.
